content.title: U.S. Government's "Illegal" Shake-Up Brings Changes For National Park Service Employees
content.text: Published Apr 4, 2026, 1:30 PM EDT Cristina Miceli is a travel news journalist who specializes in the passenger rail industry. Her passion for traveling began in 2019 when embarked on her first solo trip: a tour of the Middle East. After earning a Master’s degree in journalism, Cristina began a four-year-long trip around the world, traveling by train across three continents and offering readers insights into often underrated destinations, from Mauritania to Latvia to Gambia. Prior to contributing to TheTravel, Cristina worked as a reporter for The Cabo Sun and The Puerto Vallarta Sun in Mexico, as well as Sleepinginairports.net and Bookmundi.com. When she’s not writing, she can be found practicing Spanish guitar. On Thursday, April 2, U.S. Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum sent an email to the U.S. Interior Department's 70,000 workers, including National Park Service (NPS) employees, announcing "an important step." Although specific implementation plans remain confidential, a recent press release mentions that more NPS workers will soon be reassigned to visitor-facing roles. Park advocacy groups are now sounding the alarm, claiming that NPS sites will be negatively affected by this shift. U.S. Government's Latest Move Will Reassign More NPS Employees To Visitor-Facing Roles A park ranger hands out a map at Bryce Canyon National Park, UtahCredit: Joseph Sohm/Shutterstock According to the email sent to NPS workers, the Interior Department is about to take "an important step forward in strengthening service to the American people." The press release published on April 2 also announces key changes for NPS workers. The email also claims that the initiative reflects "a commitment to delivering faster, more reliable service to the public." In addition, the new measures will sharpen focus on "core water and power missions" while "reducing administrative burdens and improving internal operations to ensure team members have the tools and support needed to provide fast, reliable service to the public, our partners and stakeholders." The press release also mentions the advancement of responsible land and wildlife management across the country and the acceleration of the delivery of "high-quality science." This Staff Shift May Violate The National Parks Omnibus Management Act The Natural Resource Stewardship and Science Directorate (NRSS) provides "scientific, technical, and administrative support to national parks for the management of natural resources." It aims to develop, utilize, and distribute tools to help the NPS fulfill its core mission: protecting NPS sites so that they remain unimpaired for future generations. Because of this, reducing the NRSS workforce may be illegal under the National Parks Omnibus Management Act of 1998, which directs the Secretary of the Interior to "assure that management of NPS units is enhanced by the availability and utilization of a broad program of the highest quality science and information." By shifting employees from natural resource management positions to visitor-facing roles, the Trump administration may also be going against the Organic Act. The Organic Act Claims The NPS's Main Aim Is Conservation National Park Service ranger takes photo of the active volcano at the Hawaii Volcanoes National Park. Hawaii Volcanoes National Park became a national park in 1916.Credit: via Shutterstock In 1916, President Woodrow Wilson signed the Organic Act, officially establishing the NPS, whose aim was to protect the 35 national parks then in existence, as well as those yet to be established. While ensuring national parks across the country remain safe and provide services for visitors is crucial, the NPS's main aim remains to preserve these sites for future generations, which may be harder to achieve if most workers are focused on visitor-facing roles. Advocacy groups are now openly criticizing the Interior Department's latest initiative, arguing that it runs counter to the very purpose for which the NPS was created. Park Advocacy Groups Are Criticizing The Staff Shift US National Park Service (NPS) Logo at the Entrance to Zion National Park, Mountain Range in Background, Springdale, Utah, UT, USACredit: Shutterstock Emily Douce, of the National Park Conservation Association, said this move will worsen an already critical situation, since the NPS is already struggling with the loss of about 24% of its permanent staff in 2025. Similarly, Gerry James, deputy director of the Sierra Club's Outdoors For All campaign, said that, contrary to what the Interior Department claims, this is not an improvement for the NPS, a claim aligning with survey data indicating that 98% of NPS workers don't trust U.S. government leaders. "If Interior's initiative were really about serving the public better, we would see proposals for stronger staffing, deeper investment, and more support for the people who protect our public lands and welcome people into them," Gerry James declared in a statement.
